title: Ketone Body Metabolism
objectives: Understand the biosynthesis of ketone bodies in liver mitochondria
Describe the utilization of ketone bodies in peripheral tissues
Explain the physiological and pathological roles of ketogenesis
Analyze the regulation of ketone body metabolism
Identify clinical disorders related to ketone body metabolism

overview.title: Ketone Body Overview
overview.content:
Ketone bodies (acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate, and acetone) are water-soluble molecules produced from fatty acids during periods of low glucose availability. They serve as alternative energy sources for extrahepatic tissues, particularly the brain, heart, and skeletal muscle during fasting or prolonged exercise.

Biological Significance

  • Energy Carrier: Transport acetyl-CoA equivalents from liver to peripheral tissues
  • Brain Fuel: Supplies up to 70% of brain energy during prolonged fasting
  • Metabolic Flexibility: Allows survival during carbohydrate deprivation
  • Signaling Molecules: β-hydroxybutyrate functions as a histone deacetylase inhibitor

Ketone Body Species

Major Ketone Bodies

  • Acetoacetate (primary product)
  • β-Hydroxybutyrate (reduced form)
  • Acetone (spontaneous decarboxylation product)

Properties

  • Water-soluble
  • Transportable in blood without albumin
  • Cross blood-brain barrier via monocarboxylate transporters

ketogenesis.title: Ketogenesis Pathway
ketogenesis.content:
Hepatic Synthesis

Location: Liver mitochondria (matrix)

Precursor: Acetyl-CoA from β-oxidation

Key Enzymes: HMG-CoA synthase (rate-limiting), HMG-CoA lyase

Biochemical Steps

  1. 2 Acetyl-CoA → Acetoacetyl-CoA (thiolase)
  2. Acetoacetyl-CoA + Acetyl-CoA → HMG-CoA (HMG-CoA synthase)
  3. HMG-CoA → Acetoacetate + Acetyl-CoA (HMG-CoA lyase)
  4. Acetoacetate ↔ β-Hydroxybutyrate (β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase)

Regulation

Activators: Low insulin/glucagon ratio, high FFA availability, carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT1) activity

Inhibitors: High malonyl-CoA, insulin, succinyl-CoA (competes for CoA)

ketolysis.title: Ketone Body Utilization
ketolysis.content:
Extrahepatic Tissues

Brain: β-Hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase converts β-HB back to acetoacetate

Heart: Prefers ketones over glucose as fuel during fasting

Muscle: Oxidizes ketones during prolonged exercise

Activation Pathway

  1. β-Hydroxybutyrate → Acetoacetate (β-HBDH)
  2. Acetoacetate + Succinyl-CoA → Acetoacetyl-CoA + Succinate (succinyl-CoA:3-oxoacid CoA-transferase, SCOT)
  3. Acetoacetyl-CoA → 2 Acetyl-CoA (thiolase)

Energy Yield

β-Hydroxybutyrate: 21.5 ATP/molecule (vs 30 ATP/glucose)

Acetoacetate: 22.5 ATP/molecule

Efficiency: More ATP per carbon than glucose

physiological_states.title: Physiological States
physiological_states.content:
Starvation

Phase 1: Glycogen depletion (first 24 hours)

Phase 2: Gluconeogenesis predominates (days 2-3)

Phase 3: Ketosis develops (after 3 days)

Ketogenic Diet

Macronutrients: High fat (70-80%), moderate protein, very low carb (<50g/day)

Adaptation: 2-4 weeks for full keto-adaptation

Neonatal Period

Importance: Newborns rely on ketones until milk supply stabilizes

Breast Milk: High in medium-chain triglycerides (ketogenic)

clinical_correlations.title: Clinical Correlations
clinical_correlations.content:
Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)

Pathogenesis: Absolute insulin deficiency with uncontrolled lipolysis

Biochemistry: Blood ketones >5mM, pH <7.3, anion gap >12

Treatment: Insulin, fluids, electrolyte replacement

Inborn Errors

SCOT Deficiency: Inability to utilize ketones → severe hypoglycemia

HMG-CoA Lyase Deficiency: Blocks ketogenesis → hypoketotic hypoglycemia

Therapeutic Uses

Epilepsy: Ketogenic diet reduces seizure frequency

Neuroprotection: Potential in Alzheimer's, Parkinson's diseases

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
Why doesn't the liver use ketone bodies it produces?+
Liver lacks succinyl-CoA:3-oxoacid CoA-transferase (SCOT), the key enzyme for ketone body activation, making ketogenesis a one-way pathway in hepatocytes.
How does ketosis differ from ketoacidosis?+
Ketosis is controlled physiological adaptation (blood ketones 1-5mM, pH normal), while ketoacidosis is pathological (ketones >5mM with acidemia).
Why does the brain prefer glucose but can use ketones?+
Neurons normally require glucose for anaplerosis, but during starvation they express MCT transporters and enzymes to utilize ketones which preserve TCA cycle intermediates.
What causes the 'keto breath' odor?+
Acetone, the volatile ketone body, is exhaled through lungs and has a characteristic fruity smell detectable at ketone concentrations >1mM.
